en: Khuddakanikāya Dhammapada Yamakavagga (The Chapter on Pairs)
States of being are preceded by the mind, headed by the mind,
and made of the mind.
If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind,
suffering follows one from that very cause.
Like the footprints of one who draws a chariot wheel.
The Story of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī (Dhp 2).
Mind precedes all phenomena;
Mind is supreme, mind-made;
if one speaks or acts with a pure mind, [happiness follows one even as a shadow that never departs].
Then happiness follows him,
like a shadow that never leaves.
The Story of Elder Tissa (Dhp 3).
"He has struck me, he has hurt me,
he has defeated me, he has taken away what is mine"—
those who harbor such thoughts toward him, [are themselves harmed].
The truth does not satisfy them: "He abused me, he struck me,
he defeated me, he robbed me."
But those who do not harbor resentment toward them—for them, enmity subsides.
(The Story of Kāḷayakkhinī; Dhp 5, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 2)
For hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world;
it is appeased only by non-hatred.
This is the eternal law. At Kosambī:
Others do not understand.
We strive for this here;
and those who understand that therein,
from that their disputes are stilled.
The Story of the Elder Mahākāḷa (Dhp 7, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 2):
One who dwells contemplating beauty, with the sense-faculties unrestrained;
One who lacks moderation in food,
who is indolent and of inferior energy—
Māra truly overcomes such a person.
As the wind [shakes] a weak tree,
so does craving shake one who dwells contemplating the unattractive and is well-restrained in the sense faculties.
One who knows the proper measure in food,
who is endowed with faith and has aroused energy—
Māra truly cannot overcome such a person.
As the wind [shatters] a rocky mountain.
The Story of Devadatta (Dhp 9, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 3): One who has not cast off impurities [yet wears] the saffron robe...
He who wears the robe while being devoid of self-control and truth does not deserve the saffron-colored garment.
But he who has vomited out impurities,
who is well-composed in the precepts,
and is endowed with self-control and truth—
He indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.
The Story of the Elder Sāriputta (Dhp 11, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 3):
Those who perceive the essential in the unessential...
Those who see the essence in what is not essential do not attain the essence,
for their range of activity is governed by wrong intentions.
Having understood the essential as essential, and the non-essential as non-essential,
they attain the essential.
The domain of right intention.
The Story of the Elder Nanda (Dhp 13, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 4):
Just as a house with a poorly thatched roof...
Just as rain penetrates an ill-thatched house,
so does lust penetrate an untrained mind.
Just as rain does not penetrate a well-roofed house,
so too the mind that is well-cultivated—
Passion does not penetrate him.
The Story of Cunda the Sūkara (Dhp 15, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 4):
Here he grieves, and after passing away he grieves.
The evildoer grieves in both worlds;
he grieves and is tormented when he beholds his own defiled karma.
The Lay Disciple Dhammika (Dhp 16, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 4):
One rejoices here, one rejoices after passing away;
having performed merit, one rejoices in both places.
He rejoices, he exults,
having seen the purity of his own karma.
(The Story of Devadatta, Dhp 17)
Here one suffers, having passed away one suffers;
the doer of evil suffers in both places.
One suffers thinking, "Evil was done by me."
He burns all the more when gone to a state of woe.
The Story of Queen Sumanā (Dhp 18, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 5):
One rejoices here, and one rejoices after passing away;
One who has performed merit rejoices in both worlds;
they rejoice, thinking, "Merit has been done by me," and they rejoice even more when gone to a happy destination.
The Story of the Two Assistant Monks (Dhp 19, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 5):
Even if one speaks much that is well-composed, if that person is negligent and does not act accordingly, [he is like a cowherd counting another's cattle].
One who counts the cattle of others like a cowherd does not partake in the fruit of the ascetic life, even if he speaks but a little that is well-composed. (Dhp 20, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 6)
One who lives in accordance with the Dhamma,
having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
being possessed of right clear comprehension and well-liberated in mind;
Not grasping at anything here or in the world beyond,
he partakes in the fruit of asceticism.
The first chapter, the Yamaka-vagga.
Khuddakanikāya Dhammapada:
The Chapter on Heedfulness (Appamādavagga)
Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless;
heedlessness is the path of death.
Those who are heedful do not die;
those who are heedless are as if already dead.
Having understood this distinction, (Dhp 22, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 7)
The wise delight in heedfulness;
they rejoice in heedfulness,
finding pleasure in the domain of the Noble Ones.
Those wise ones, meditative and constant,
always firm in their exertion,
attain Nibbāna.
The unsurpassed security from bondage.
The Story of the Merchant Kumbaghosaka (Dhp 24, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 7):
For one who is industrious and mindful,
For one who performs good deeds with reflection,
who is self-controlled, lives according to the Dhamma,
and is diligent, their fame increases.
By exertion, by heedfulness, by restraint,
and by self-control;
Let the wise man make for himself an island,
which the flood cannot overwhelm.
(The Story of the Proclamation of the Auspicious Day of the Fools)
Fools of little intelligence devote themselves to negligence,
whereas the wise person devotes himself to heedfulness.
He guards his wealth like the best of treasures.
Do not indulge in negligence, nor in intimacy with sensual pleasures.
For by meditating with diligence, one attains abundant happiness.
The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa (Dhp 28, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 8)
When the wise person dispels negligence with diligence,
having ascended the palace of wisdom,
The sorrowless one looks upon the grieving people;
like one standing on a mountain looking down at those on the ground,
the wise man observes the foolish.
The Story of the Monk Who Was a Friend to Both the Negligent and the Diligent (Dhp 29, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 9):
Heedful among the heedless, wide awake among those who sleep;
As a swift horse leaves behind a weak one, so does the wise man depart, leaving [the world] behind.
(Maghavatthu; Dhp 30, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 9)
Through heedfulness,
Maghavā attained preeminence among the gods;
they praise heedfulness.
Heedlessness is always censured.
(The Case of a Certain Bhikkhu, Dhp 31, PTS 2nd ed.
Dhp 9) The bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness,
Or one who sees danger in negligence,
goes forth like a fire, burning away fetters both subtle and gross.
The Story of the Elder Tissa, Dweller in the Market Town (Dhp 32, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 9):
A bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness and sees danger in negligence;
One is incapable of falling away;
one is close to Nibbāna itself.
This is the second chapter, on Heedfulness.
Khuddakanikāya Dhammapada Cittavagga (The Chapter on the Mind)
The mind is flickering and fickle,
difficult to guard and hard to restrain.
The wise man makes himself straight,
just as a fletcher straightens his arrow; like a lotus cast upon dry land.
Rising up from Okamokata,
this mind quivers;
it must abandon Māra’s realm.
The story of a certain bhikkhu (Dhp 35, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 10):
Of that which is difficult to restrain, light, and falling wherever it pleases;
The taming of the mind is good;
a tamed mind brings happiness.
The Case of a Certain Discontented Bhikkhu (Dhp 36, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 10)
The wise person should guard the mind, which is extremely difficult to see, exceedingly subtle, and capable of falling wherever it desires.
The mind, when guarded, brings happiness.
(The Story of the Elder Saṅgharakkhitabhāgineyya; Dhp 37, PTS 2nd ed.
Dhp 11) It wanders far and travels alone.
Bodiless and dwelling in the cave,
those who restrain the mind will be released from the bonds of Māra.
For one whose mind is unsteady, who does not understand the true Dhamma; (Dhp 38, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 11)
For one whose confidence wavers, wisdom does not reach fulfillment;
for one whose mind is not free from lust. (Dhp 39, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 11)
For one whose mind is unassailed,
who has abandoned both merit and evil,
there is no fear for the vigilant.
Having understood this body to be like a water-pot,
and having established this mind to be like a city;
Fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom;
guard what has been won, and remain without attachment.
(The Story of the Elder Tiṣya with the Putrid Limbs, Dhp 41)
Soon indeed this body will lie upon the earth,
discarded and devoid of consciousness.
Like a useless block of wood.
The Story of Nanda the Cowherd (Dhp 42, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 12):
Whatever one might do in every direction—
Or even an enemy toward an enemy—
a mind wrongly directed makes one worse than that.
Neither mother nor father would do that,
nor would any other kinsmen.
A mind rightly directed will make him even better than that.
The third chapter on the Mind is finished.
Khuddakanikāya Dhammapada Pupphavagga (The Chapter on Flowers)
The Story of the Five Hundred Monks Absorbed in Discourse on the Earth (Dhp 44, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 13):
Who will traverse this earth, and this world of Yama together with its gods?
Who, being skilled, will weave together the well-taught verses of the Dhamma like a flower?
The trainee shall traverse the earth. (Dhp 45, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 13)
The disciple who is still in training, having well-expounded the verses of Dhamma,
will skillfully scatter them throughout this world of Yama and its gods, just as one scatters flowers.
Having understood this body to be like a bubble of foam,
and having fully awakened to its nature as a mirage;
Having cut off Māra’s flowering blossoms,
one shall go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
(Viṭaṭūbha’s Story, Dhp 47)
Just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village, so does death carry off the man who plucks flowers, his mind distracted.
Death carries one away.
The Story of the Maiden Patipūjikā (Dhp 48). While one is still plucking flowers, death seizes that person.
The Ender brings under his control the man whose mind is distracted and who remains unsated with sensual pleasures.
The Story of the Merchant Macchariya-Kosiya (Dhp 49, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 14):
Just as a bee, without harming the color or fragrance of a flower, [takes its nectar].
Taking only its flavor, it passes away;
thus should the sage fare in the village.
(The Story of the Ājīvaka from Pāveyya, Dhp 50)
One should not look at the faults of others,
nor at what others have done or left undone; one should examine only oneself.
Both those done and those not yet done.
The Story of the Lay Follower Chattapāṇi (Dhp 51):
Just as a beautiful flower,
Beautiful in color but lacking fragrance;
even so, well-spoken words are fruitless for one who does not act upon them.
Just as a beautiful flower is both colorful and fragrant,
so too are well-spoken words.
It is fruitful for one who exerts effort.
The Story of Visākhā (Dhp 53, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 15):
Just as from a heap of flowers...
One should make many garlands;
likewise, by one born as a mortal,
much that is wholesome should be done.
The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor does that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine; but the fragrance of virtue goes even against the wind. (Dhp 54)
The fragrance of the virtuous wafts against the wind;
the person of integrity pervades all directions.
Whether it be sandalwood or tagara—(Dhp 55, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 16)
The blue lotus and the jasmine—
of all these varieties of fragrance,
the fragrance of virtue is unsurpassed.
The Story of the Alms-Giving to the Elder Mahākassapa (Dhp 56, PTS 2nd ed.
Dhp 16) Faint is this fragrance,
which comes from tagara and sandalwood;
But the fragrance of those who possess virtue wafts supreme even among the gods.
The Story of the Parinibbāna of the Elder Godhika (Dhp 57, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 16)
For those who are perfected in virtue,
who dwell in heedfulness,
and who are liberated through right knowledge—
Māra does not find the path.
The Story of Garahadatta (Dhp 58, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 16):
Just as in a heap of refuse...
In that great highway where [the body] has been abandoned,
a lotus would grow there—
purely fragrant and delightful.
Thus, among those who have become like a heap of refuse,
among the worldlings who are blind,
he outshines them all with his wisdom.
A disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Fourth Chapter on Flowers.
The Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
The Way of the Truth-Sayings, Chapter on Fools,
Story of a Certain Man (Dhp 60, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 17)
Long is the night for one who is awake;
long is the league for one who is weary;
long is saṃsāra for the foolish.
For those who do not understand the true Dhamma.
The Story of Mahākassapa’s Co-resident (Dhp 61, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 17):
If, while wandering, one does not find [the goal],...
One should make one's own conduct similar to that;
one should practice resolute solitary wandering,
for there is no companionship with fools.
"I have sons, I have wealth"— thus the fool is distressed.
For one has no self belonging to oneself;
how then can there be sons? How can there be wealth?
(The Story of the Robber who Cut Open a Knot)
The fool who perceives himself as a fool is thereby wise;
but the fool who fancies himself wise—
He indeed is called a "fool.
The Story of the Elder Udāyin (Dhp 64, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 18):
Even if a fool lives for as long as life lasts...
One who waits upon a wise person does not understand the Dhamma,
just as a spoon does not know the taste of the soup.
If a wise person attends upon one who is learned for even a moment, [he gains great benefit].
One quickly understands the Dhamma, just as the tongue perceives the flavor of soup.
The Story of Suppabuddha the Leper (Dhp 66, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 18)
Fools of poor intelligence wander about as if they were their own enemies,
performing evil deeds.
Whatever results in bitter fruit— that deed,
though performed, is not good. (The Farmer’s Story,
Dhp 67) It is not a deed well done.
That which, having done, one regrets;
the fruit of which one experiences while weeping with a tearful face.
That deed is well done which, having been done, one does not regret.
Just like the garland-maker Sumanā.
He whose mind is joyful and delighted experiences the fruit [of his merit].
The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā (Dhp 69, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 19)
The fool considers it honey as long as the evil does not ripen;
but when the evil ripens, [he suffers].
Then one encounters suffering.
The Story of the Elder Jambuka (Dhp 70, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 19):
Month after month, with the tip of a blade of kusa grass...
A fool might eat his meal,
yet he is not worth even a sixteenth part of those who have realized the Dhamma.
For an evil deed that has been committed does not simply vanish,
like milk mixed with water.
It follows the fool as he burns, like fire covered by ashes.
The Story of the Sixty-Peaked Petas (Dhp 72, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 20)
As long as knowledge arises for a fool, it leads only to his harm;
it destroys the fool’s bright side.
Shattering his head.
The Story of the Householder Citta (Dhp 73).
One should desire the cultivation of what is non-existent.
Preeminence among the monks,
authority over monasteries,
and honor from other families.
"Let both householders and those gone forth alike think, 'He has done this for me';
let them be entirely under my influence."
Regarding whatever duties or non-duties there may be—
such is the intention of the fool,
and his desire and pride increase.
The means for acquiring gain is one thing, while that which leads to Nibbāna is another.
Having thus understood this through direct knowledge,
a monk who is a disciple of the Buddha should not delight in honor.
One should cultivate discernment.
The fifth chapter, on the Fools,
from the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Dhammapada, Chapter on the Wise (Paṇḍitavagga), The Story of the Elder Rādha (Dhp 76, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 22) The wise person, having understood the Dhamma well-taught by the Noble One, dwells with reverence and heedfulness; he does not fall away from that which is wholesome. The fool, however, who does not understand the Dhamma well-taught by the Noble One, dwells without reverence and heedlessness; he falls away from that which is wholesome.
One who sees faults, who speaks with restraint, and who is wise— one should regard such a person as one who reveals hidden treasures.
One should associate with such a wise person;
for one who associates with such a person,
it becomes better, not worse.
One should advise and instruct, and restrain one from what is unwholesome.
For he is dear to the virtuous, but is disliked by the wicked.
The Story of Elder Channa (Dhp 78, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 22)
Do not associate with evil friends;
do not associate with the lowest of men;
one should associate with virtuous friends.
One should devote oneself to the Supreme Person.
The Elder Mahākappina’s Story (Dhp 79, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 22):
One who finds joy in the Dhamma sleeps happily.
With a serene mind,
the wise person always delights in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.
For irrigators lead the water with canals, and fletchers straighten the arrow-shaft; just so do the wise train themselves.
Carpenters shape wood;
the wise subdue themselves.
(The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya) (Dhp 81, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 23)
Just as a solid block of rock is not shaken by the wind,
so too [the sage] remains unmoved amidst blame and praise.
The wise do not shrink back.
The Story of Kāṇamātā (Dhp 82, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 23):
Just as a deep lake...
Clear and undisturbed;
having heard the Dhammas in this way,
the wise become serene.
The Story of the Five Hundred Monks (Dhp 83, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 23):
In every circumstance, indeed, the virtuous relinquish all;
the holy ones, desiring no sensual pleasures, do not prattle for their sake.
Whether touched by happiness or by suffering, the wise do not display elation or dejection.
(The Story of the Elder Dhammika; Dhp 84, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 24)
Neither for one's own sake nor for the sake of another,
nor should one desire a son, nor wealth, nor a kingdom; one should not,
by means of unrighteousness, desire the success of oneself.
He should be virtuous, wise, and righteous.
Regarding the Elder who Listens to the Dhamma (Dhp 85, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 24):
Few among humans...
Those people who go to the further shore,
while this other generation merely runs along the near bank.
But those people who follow the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma as it has been rightly proclaimed,
they shall go to the further shore.
The realm of Death is so difficult to cross.
[The Story of the Five Hundred Guest Monks] (Dhp 87, PTS 2nd ed.
Dhp 24) Having utterly abandoned dark states,
Let the wise person cultivate purity,
having gone from home to homelessness,
to a secluded place that is difficult to access.
One should desire delight therein,
having abandoned sensual pleasures and possessing nothing;
one should purify oneself.
The wise one [is freed] from the defilements of the mind—
those whose minds are rightly well-developed in the factors of enlightenment.
Those who delight in the relinquishing of grasping, being without clinging—
having exhausted the taints, they are radiant.
They have attained final nibbāna in the world.
The sixth chapter, on the Wise, is concluded.
[From the] Khuddakanikāya.
The Chapter on Arahants,

The Story of the Questions of Jīvaka (Dhp 90, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 26) “Even though one may live for a hundred years, heedless and uncontrolled, better it is to live for a single day of one who is mindful and self-controlled.”
For one who has traversed the path, who is free from sorrow,
who is liberated in every respect,
and for whom all fetters have been abandoned—
No fever exists for them.
The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa (Dhp 91, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 26):
Those who possess mindfulness exert themselves;
They do not delight in a dwelling;
like swans that have left a pond,
they abandon home after home.
The Story of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa (Dhp 92, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 26):
Those who have no hoarding, who have fully understood food;
For those whose sphere of activity is the void and the signless liberation,
like birds in the sky—
Their destination is difficult to trace.
The Story of the Elder Anuruddha (Dhp 93, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 26):
He whose taints are utterly destroyed...
And not dependent on nutriment;
for whom liberation— both empty and signless— is the range of experience.
Like the track of birds in the sky, his path is difficult to trace.
The Story of the Elder Mahākaccāyana (Dhp 94, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 27)
He whose faculties have attained tranquility,
like well-tamed horses by a skilled charioteer—
he who has abandoned conceit and is free from taints.
Even the gods envy such a one as he.
The Story of the Elder Sāriputta (Dhp 95).
Like the earth, he is not disturbed.
Such a one of excellent vows is like an indakhīla pillar;
like a lake free from mud,
for such a one, there are no further rounds of saṃsāra.
Tranquil is his mind, and tranquil are his speech and action.
Of one who is liberated through perfect knowledge,
who is tranquil and steadfast—
this was the story of the Elder Sāriputta (Dhp 97).
The man who lacks faith, who is ungrateful,
and who has severed the bond of continuity—
his opportunity is destroyed, his hope is vomited out.
He is indeed the supreme person.
The Story of the Elder Revata of the Acacia Grove (Dhp 98, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 28):
Whether in the village or in the forest, he is truly a sage.
Whether in the water or on dry land,
wherever the Arahants dwell—
that ground is delightful.
Delightful are the forest groves,
where people find no pleasure.
Those free from passion will delight [in this], not those who seek sensual pleasures.
The seventh chapter: The Chapter on the Arahants.
Khuddakanikāya Dhammapada Sahassavagga (The Chapter on the Thousand)
Even a thousand words, if they are composed of meaningless phrases; (as in the case of the robber-killer Tambadāṭhika).
A single meaningful word is better, hearing which one attains peace.
(The Story of the Elder Bahiya Daruciriya; Dhp 101, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 29)
Even a thousand verses composed of meaningless words are not worth a single verse-line that is meaningful.
Having heard which, one becomes tranquil.
The Story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī (Dhp 102, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 29):
One who might recite a hundred verses, yet...
Better than a hundred meaningless words is a single word of Dhamma,
hearing which one attains peace.
One might conquer a thousand men in battle, each with a thousand others, yet it is better to conquer oneself alone.
He is indeed the supreme victor in battle.
The Story of the Brahmin Who Asked About Harm (Dhp 104, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 30):
"Victory over oneself is indeed better."
And whatever other people there may be,
they do not equal the person who has tamed themselves,
who always conducts themselves with restraint.
Neither a god nor a gandhabba,
nor Māra together with Brahmā,
could turn what has been won into a defeat.
For such a person as this.
The Story of the Brahmin Uncle of the Elder Sāriputta (Dhp 106, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 30):
"Month after month, with a thousand [pieces of gold]..."
If one were to sacrifice for a hundred years to a hundred [ordinary] persons,
yet were to honor for even a moment a single person whose self is cultivated—
That very act of worship is better than an offering made for a hundred years.
The Story of the Nephew of the Elder Sāriputta (Dhp 107, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 30)
Though a person might tend a fire in the forest for a hundred years,
[it is better than honoring] even a single person of developed self.
One should worship for even a moment;
that very act of worship is better than an offering made for a hundred years.
Whatever sacrifice or offering one might perform in the world for a year, seeking merit, [is not worth a sixteenth part of the merit gained by honoring those who have realized the Truth].
All that does not equal even a fourth part of the merit gained by bowing down to those who are upright;
honoring those who have attained rectitude is superior. (The Story of the Youth Āyuvaḍḍhana, Dhp 109, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 31)
For one who is habitually respectful and always honors the elders,
four qualities increase:
Long life, beauty, happiness, and strength— As for one who lives for a hundred years, [The story of the novice Saṅkicca; Dhp 110, PTS (2nd ed.
Dhp 31] Whoever might live for a hundred years...
Better for a single day the life of one who is virtuous and meditative than that of one who is immoral and unconcentrated.
Though one may live for a hundred years, if one is witless and unconcentrated;
A single day’s life of one who is wise and meditative is better than a hundred years of one who is otherwise.
(The Story of the Elder Sabbadāsa; Dhp 112, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 32)
Better than living for a hundred years,
lazy and lacking in energy,
is to live for a single day.
Exerting firm energy.
The Story of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā (Dhp 113, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 32):
Even if one should live for a hundred years...
Not seeing rise and fall,
a single day lived seeing rise and fall is better.
Though one should live for a hundred years without seeing the deathless state, it would be better to live for a single day seeing the deathless state.
A single day of life is better for one who beholds the deathless state.
The Story of the Elder Nun Bahuputtikā (Dhp 115, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 32)
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dhamma is to live for a single day.
Having seen the supreme Dhamma.
The eighth chapter: The Thousand.
The Minor Collection.

The Chapter on Evil: The Story of the Brahmin Cūḷekasāṭaka (Dhp 116, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 33) One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "this is not known by anyone," does not escape from that evil; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "no one sees me," is seen by the gods; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "I am alone, there is no second," is accompanied by his own deeds; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "I am alone, there is no witness," is witnessed by his own deeds; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "I am alone, there is no one to know," is known by his own deeds; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "I am alone, there is no one to see," is seen by his own deeds; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "I am alone, there is no one to hear," is heard by his own deeds; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "I am alone, there is no one to speak of," is spoken of by his own deeds; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "I am alone, there is no one to remember," is remembered by his own deeds; for the deed follows after him. One who has committed evil deeds, thinking "I am alone, there is no one to question," is questioned by his own deeds; for the deed follows after him. One should take delight in that;

Do not despise evil, thinking,

Do not despise small merit, thinking,

By the falling of a single drop of water,

Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean,

For one who is completely free from passion, there is no sorrow; whence could there be fear?
The Story of Prince Anitthigandha (Dhp 215, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 61)
From desire arises sorrow,
from desire arises fear; for one who is completely free from desire, [there is neither sorrow nor fear].
There is no sorrow; whence could there be fear?
(The Story of a Certain Brahmin, Dhp 216, PTS 2nd ed.
Dhp 61) Sorrow is born of craving.
From craving fear is born;
for one who is completely free from craving,
there is no sorrow— how, then, could there be fear?
The Story of the Five Hundred Boys (Dhp 217, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 62):
One endowed with virtue and vision, established in the Dhamma, and a knower of truth;
A person performs their own karma; that very karma makes them dear.
The Story of the Elder Ekānāgāmin (Dhp 218, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 62)
Born of passion for the unproclaimed,
yet touched by the mind;
with a heart unattached to sensual pleasures—
He is called "one who flows upwards.
The Foundation of Delight (Dhp 219, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 62):
"A man who has been long away..."
Having returned safely from afar,

In the same way, when one who has performed meritorious deeds passes from this world to the next,

Like a beloved kinsman who has returned.
The sixteenth chapter: The Chapter on the Beloved.
From the *Khuddakanikāya*.

The Dhammapada, Chapter on Anger: The Story of the Kṣatriya Girl Rohiṇī (Dhp 221, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 63) Even as a mother protects her son with her life, so should one cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. Just as a father protects his only son, so should one cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. Toward all living creatures, both those that are weak and those that are strong, one should cultivate a boundless heart. One should cultivate a boundless heart toward the entire world, above, below, and across, unobstructed, free from enmity, and without ill will. Standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, as long as one is awake, one should be devoted to this mindfulness; this, they say, is the teaching of the Noble Ones. One who dwells thus with a mind constantly concentrated attains peace of mind here and now. This, they say, is the teaching of the Noble Ones.
One should abandon anger and relinquish conceit;
one should transcend all fetters.
Such a person, not clinging to name-and-form—
Sufferings do not overcome one who possesses nothing.
The Story of a Certain Bhikkhu (Dhp 222, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 63):
Whoever indeed [subdues] anger as soon as it has arisen...
I call him a charioteer who can restrain a racing chariot;
others are merely those who hold the reins.
The Story of the Laywoman Uttarā (Dhp 223):
Conquer anger with non-anger;
conquer the wicked with goodness.
One should conquer the miser with generosity, and the speaker of falsehood with truth.
The Story of the Question of Mahāmoggallāna (Dhp 224, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 63)
One should speak the truth, one should not be angry,
and one should give even a little when asked;
by these three points, [one is established].
Let him go into the presence of the gods.
The Story of the Brahmin Buddha’s Father (Dhp 225).
Those sages who are non-violent...
Those who are constantly restrained in body go to the deathless state,
where having gone, they do not grieve.
For those who are ever vigilant and train themselves day and night, (there is no suffering).
For those who are intent upon Nibbāna, the taints come to an end.
The Story of the Lay Follower Atula (Dhp 227, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 64)
This is ancient, O Incomparable One;
it is not as it is today:
they blame one who sits in silence.
They blame the one who speaks much;
they also blame the one who speaks sparingly;
there is no one in the world who is not blamed.
There has never been, there will never be,
nor is there now found,
a person who is entirely blameworthy.
Or one who is praised unreservedly.
That which the wise praise—having investigated it day after day—(Dhp 229, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 65)
The wise person, whose conduct is flawless and who is established in wisdom and virtue,
is like a coin of pure Jambūnada gold.
Who is worthy to blame him?
Even the gods praise him;
he is praised even by Brahmā.
One should guard against bodily provocation and be restrained in body. (Chabbaggiya-vatthu, Dhp 231; PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 65)
Abandoning misconduct of body,
one should practice good conduct with the body;
one should guard against verbal anger.
One should be restrained in speech;
having abandoned verbal misconduct,
one should practice good conduct of speech.
One should guard against mental provocation,
be restrained in mind,
and having abandoned mental misconduct, [one should dwell in purity].
One should practice good conduct with the mind.
The wise are restrained in body and likewise restrained in speech.
The wise who are restrained in mind are indeed well-restrained in every way.

The Minor Collection:
The Dhammapada,
Chapter on Defilements (Malavagga)
Like a withered leaf, you are now at the end; the messengers of Yama have already arrived for you.
You stand at the point of departure, yet you possess no provisions for the journey.
Therefore, make an island for yourself. (Dhp 236, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 67)
Exert yourself quickly and become wise;
having shaken off impurities and being free from blemish,
you will reach the divine ground of the Noble Ones.
Your youth has now departed,
and you have come into the presence of Yama;
there is no dwelling for you in between.
And you have no provisions for the journey. Make an island for yourself;
exert yourself quickly and become wise.
With taints removed and free from blemish, you shall not again undergo birth and old age.
(The Story of a Certain Brahmin; Dhp 239, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 68)
Gradually, little by little, moment by moment, the wise person,
like a smith working silver, [purifies themselves].
Wash away the stain from yourself.
The Story of the Elder Tissa (Dhp 240).
Just as rust arises from iron, so does defilement arise from the self.
Satisfied, it devours that very [creature];
so too, one’s own deeds lead the one who behaves with excessive license to a state of misery.
Lāḷudāyī’s Story (Dhp 241):
Recitation is the impurity of mantras;
lack of exertion is the impurity of households.
Laziness is the stain of beauty;
negligence is the stain of one who guards [virtue]. (Dhp 242, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 69)
Evil conduct is the stain of a woman,
stinginess is the stain of one who gives;
indeed, evil states are stains.
In this world and in the next,
there is a stain more foul than all others:
ignorance is the supreme stain.
Having abandoned this stain,
O bhikkhus, be stainless.
(The Story of the Bhikkhu Cūḷasāri, Dhp 244)
Easy to live with is one who is shameless,
bold as a crow, treacherous,
intrusive, and impudent.
Life is lived with defilement;
it is difficult for one who possesses a sense of shame, who constantly seeks purity, to live [a life of such integrity].
By one who is secluded, not arrogant, pure in livelihood, and discerning—
(The Five Subjects for Laymen, Dhp 246, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 69).
He who takes the life of a living being,
speaks falsehood,
and takes what is not given in this world—
He goes to another's wife, and that man who is devoted to the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors; (Dhp 247, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 70)
Right here in this very world, he digs up his own root.
Know this, O man! (Dhp 248, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 70)
Of evil nature and unrestrained;
let not greed and unrighteousness subject you to long-lasting suffering.
Indeed, people give according to their faith and according to their confidence.
In this regard, he who becomes dejected over the food and drink of others,
neither by day nor by night, [finds peace].
One attains concentration.
For one by whom this [craving] has been utterly cut off,
destroyed at the root, and uprooted;
Whether by day or by night, he indeed attains concentration.
(The Case of the Five Lay Followers, Dhp 251, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 71)
There is no fire like lust,
no grip like hatred,
and no snare like delusion.
There is no river equal to craving.
[The Story of the Merchant Meṇḍaka] (Dhp 252, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 71):
It is easy to see the faults of others, but...
But his own faults are difficult to see;
for he winnows the faults of others like chaff.
But he conceals his own [faults], like a deceitful gambler hiding a losing throw.
(The Story of the Elder Ujjhānasaññin; Dhp 253, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 71)
For one who observes the faults of others and is constantly preoccupied with finding fault,
the taints increase.
He is far from the destruction of the taints.

There is no ascetic outside [the Buddha's teaching];
people delight in conceptual proliferation (*papañca*),
while the Tathāgatas are free from proliferation.
There is no track in the sky, there is no ascetic outside [the Buddhist fold],
and conditioned phenomena are not eternal.
There is no wavering in the Buddhas.

Dhammapada, Chapter on the Foundation of Dhamma, Story of the High Court Justice (Dhp 256, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 73) The high court justice, having committed evil deeds, Was reborn in hell because of his own actions. But the one who does good deeds here, Will experience happiness in the other world.
One does not stand firm in the Dhamma by pursuing one's own interest through force; rather,
he who [discerns] both what is beneficial and what is harmful—
The wise person should discern both:
he leads others by means of justice that is free from violence and impartial.
The wise one who guards the Dhamma is called "one established in the Dhamma.
(Chabbaggiya-vatthu, Dhp 258; PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 73)
One does not become wise merely by speaking much; one who is secure,
free from enmity, and fearless— [he is wise].
“He is called wise.
The Story of One Who Exhausted the Taints with a Single Gift (Dhp 259, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 73):
One is not a bearer of the Dhamma merely by that much.
It matters not how much one speaks;
rather, it is one who, having heard even a little of the Dhamma,
perceives it with the body.
He indeed is a bearer of the Dhamma who does not neglect the Dhamma.
The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya (Dhp 260, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 73)
One does not become an elder merely because one's head is gray;
his age is simply ripe.
“He is called one who has aged in vain,” it is said.
In whom there is truth and the Dhamma, non-violence, self-restraint, and self-mastery; (Dhp 261, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 73)
He who has indeed cast off impurity and is wise is called an "Elder" (thera).
(The Story of Many Bhikkhus; Dhp 262, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 74)
A person does not become a man of noble character merely through eloquence or through the beauty of his complexion.
Envious, stingy, and deceitful—
[he] for whom this has been utterly cut off,
uprooted by the roots, and destroyed.
The wise man who has abandoned faults is called "one of noble character.
(The Story of Hatthaka; Dhp 264, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 74)
One is not a recluse by virtue of being shaven-headed,
nor one who speaks falsehoods while lacking self-restraint;
one who is possessed by desire and greed [is no recluse].
What will he be who is a recluse?
He who restrains all evils, both subtle and gross, in every way.
Because he has stilled evil things, he is called a "recluse" (*samaṇa*).
The Story of a Certain Brahmin (Dhp 266, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 75)
One does not become a bhikkhu merely by begging from others; having adopted the way of a householder, one is not thereby a bhikkhu.
One is not yet a bhikkhu by that much alone.
But he who, having cast out both merit and evil, lives the holy life here—(Dhp 267, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 75)
He who wanders through the world having fully understood it—
he indeed is called a "bhikkhu.
(Titthiyavatthu, Dhp 268)
One does not become a sage by silence,
being dull-witted and ignorant; but he who,
like one holding a scale, [weighs both sides]...
Having taken up the superior choice, the wise man avoids all evils; because of that,
he is a sage, a true silent one.
One who understands both worlds is therefore called a "muni.
(The Story of the Fisherman, Dhp 270)
One does not become noble by harming living beings;
non-violence toward all living beings—
“He is called ‘noble.
The case of a monk endowed with many virtues and other qualities (Dhp 271, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 76):
Not by mere virtue and observance...
Or else by great learning,
or by the attainment of concentration,
or by dwelling in seclusion.
I touch the bliss of renunciation, which is not practiced by ordinary people;
let the bhikkhu place his trust in this.
Not having reached the destruction of the taints.
The nineteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Foundation of Dhamma.
From the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Dhammapada, Chapter on the Path, Story of the Five Hundred Monks (Dhp 273, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 77) The five hundred bhikkhus, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, attained arahantship. They then rose into the air and performed various miracles. Seeing this, the people were filled with wonder and cried out: "The disciples of the Blessed One possess great power and majesty! Hearing this, the Blessed One said to the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, it is not through such displays of psychic power that one is called a true disciple of the Buddha. But he who has abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and has reached the destruction of suffering—he is truly my disciple. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own; the person who is intent on neither his own welfare nor the welfare of others; and the person who is intent on both his own welfare and the welfare of others. Of these, the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is like a man who, having climbed a tree for the sake of fruit, is shaken by fear when a monkey climbs up and plucks the fruit. He is intent on saving himself but not on saving the monkey. The person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own is like a man who, having climbed a tree for the sake of fruit, is shaken by fear when a monkey climbs up and plucks the fruit. He is intent on saving the monkey but not on saving himself. The person who is intent on neither his own welfare nor the welfare of others is like a man who, having climbed a tree for the sake of fruit, is shaken by fear when a monkey climbs up and plucks the fruit. He is intent on saving neither himself nor the monkey. But the person who is intent on both his own welfare and the welfare of others is like a man who, having climbed a tree for the sake of fruit, is shaken by fear when a monkey climbs up and plucks the fruit. He is intent on saving both himself and the monkey. He will first secure the branch for himself and then, using a rope or a stick, he will drive the monkey away. Thus, he is intent on both his own welfare and the welfare of others. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose into the air and returned to the Jetavana monastery. The bhikkhus, having heard the Dhamma, were uplifted and rejoiced in what was said by the Blessed One.
Of paths, the Eightfold is best;
of truths, the Four Noble Truths;
of all phenomena, dispassion is best.
And for the Visionary among bipeds—
this alone is the path, and no other,
for the purification of vision.
Practice this, for it is the delusion of Māra.
For by practicing this, you—(Dhp 275, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 77)
You shall make an end of suffering;
the path for piercing the thorn of ignorance has been declared to you by me.
You yourselves must exert effort;
the Tathāgatas are merely teachers.
Those who practice will be liberated.
The meditators are released from the bonds of Māra.
Regarding the characteristic of impermanence: “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. (Dhp 277, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 78)
When one sees with wisdom,
then one becomes disenchanted with suffering;
this is the path to purification.
“All conditioned phenomena are suffering”—
when one sees this with wisdom;
Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering;
this is the path to purification.
(The Basis for the Characteristic of Non-Self, Dhp 279, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 78)
“When one sees with wisdom that ‘all phenomena are non-self,’ then one becomes disenchanted with suffering.”
This is the path to purification.
The Story of the Elder Tissa the Striver: One who does not exert himself at the time for exertion... (Dhp 280, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 78).
A youth who is strong yet overcome by indolence,
whose mind and intentions are lax and who is lazy— such a person, being idle,
does not find the path through wisdom.
Guarded in speech, well-restrained in mind,
one should not commit any unwholesome deed with the body.
One should purify these three paths of action and realize the path proclaimed by the Seer of the Sages.
The Story of the Elder Poṭṭhila (Dhp 282, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 79)
Through yoga, indeed, much is born;
through non-yoga, much is destroyed.
Having understood this twofold path,
For existence and for non-existence;
one should thus settle oneself so that wisdom increases further and further.
Cut down the forest, not the tree; from the forest fear is born. (Pañcamahallaka-bhikkhu-vatthu, Dhp 283)
Having cut through both the forest and the undergrowth,
become free from the forest, O monks.
For as long as the undergrowth is not severed, (Dhp 284, PTS (2nd ed) Dhp 80)
As long as a man’s mind is attached even slightly to women,
he is like a suckling calf toward its mother.
Cut off your own affection, as one would pluck an autumnal lily with the hand.
Cultivate only the path to peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.
The Story of the Wealthy Merchant (Dhp 286, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 80)
"I shall dwell here for the rains,
here during the winter and summer"—
thus the fool deliberates.
One does not perceive the obstacle.
The Story of Kisāgotamī (Dhp 287, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 81):
"That infatuation with children and cattle..."
Death carries away the man whose mind is distracted,
just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
The Story of Paṭācārā (Dhp 288):
Sons are no refuge,
nor is a father, nor even kinsmen.
For one seized by the End-maker, there is no protection among kinsmen.
Knowing this fact, (Dhp 289, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 81)
The wise person, restrained by virtue,
shall quickly purify the path leading to Nibbāna.
The Twentieth Chapter:
On the Path. *Dhammapada*, Minor Collection (*Khuddakanikāya*).
Pakiṇṇakavagga:
The Story of One’s Own Former Deeds (Dhp 290, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 82).
By the relinquishing of even a small amount of pleasure...
Let the wise person pass over this limited pleasure; seeing the vast pleasure,
let him relinquish the pleasure of the senses.
The Story of the One Who Eats Chicken Eggs (Dhp 291, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 82):
One who seeks his own happiness by inflicting suffering upon others—
One who is entangled in association with hatred is not released from hatred.
(The Case of the Bhikkhus of Bhaddiya, Dhp 292, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 82)
For when what ought to be done is neglected,
and what ought not to be done is performed,
by those who are arrogant and heedless—
Their taints increase,
but for those in whom mindfulness directed to the body is constantly and well-undertaken, their taints are destroyed.
They do not pursue what should not be done,
but act with persistence in what should be done—
those who are mindful and clearly comprehending.
The taints come to an end.
The Story of Bhaddiya the Dwarf (Dhp 294):
Having slain mother and father,
Having slain the kings and the two kṣatriyas, along with the kingdom and its followers,
the brahmin goes on untroubled.
Having slain mother and father,
and two righteous kings,
and having slain a tiger as the fifth—
The Brahmin goes free from distress.
(The Story of the Son of the Wood-Cart Maker; Dhp 296, PTS 2nd ed.
Dhp 83) They awaken to a true awakening.
The disciples of Gotama are always those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Buddha, by day and by night.
The disciples of Gotama always awaken to a true awakening,
they for whom [this practice] occurs by day and by night.
Their mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Dhamma.
The disciples of Gotama always awaken with a true awakening.
Those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Saṅgha by day and by night awaken with a true awakening. (Dhp 299, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 84)
The disciples of Gotama are always [happy],
for whom mindfulness directed to the body is constant, both by day and by night.
The disciples of Gotama always awaken to a true awakening, both by day and by night, for those who— (Dhp 300, PTS [2nd ed] Dhp 84)
The minds of those who delight in non-violence always awaken to a true awakening;
such are the disciples of Gotama.
Those whose minds delight in meditative development by day and by night—
The Story of the Bhikkhu Vajjiputta (Dhp 302, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 84)
Difficult is the going forth, difficult is the delight [in it];
houses are hard to dwell in and full of suffering;
painful is living together with others.
The wanderer is pursued by suffering;
therefore, one should not be a wanderer,
nor should one be pursued by suffering.
The Story of the Householder Citta (Dhp 303, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 84):
Endowed with faith and perfected in virtue, he was possessed of fame and wealth.
To whatever place he goes, there he is honored.
The Story of Cūḷasubhaddā (Dhp 304, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 85)
The virtuous shine from afar,
like the Himalaya mountain;
the wicked are not seen here at all.
Like arrows shot in the night.
The Story of the Elder Ekavihārin (Dhp 305, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 85):
Sitting alone, lying down alone...
Wandering alone and untiring,
taming oneself, one should find delight at the edge of the forest.
The Twenty-first Chapter: Miscellaneous.
*Dhammapada*, Minor Collection (*Khuddakanikāya*).
The Chapter on Hell:
The Case of the Wanderer Sundarī (Dhp 306).
One who speaks what is untrue goes to hell.
Or he who, having done [an evil deed], says "I did not do it"—
both of these, upon passing away,
become equal in the next world, those men of base actions.
The Case of One Oppressed by the Fruit of Evil Conduct (Dhp 307, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 86):
Many with saffron robes around their necks are of evil character and unrestrained.
Through evil deeds, the wicked are reborn in hell.
(The Case of the Bhikkhus from the Banks of the Vaggumudā, Dhp 308, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 86)
Better it would be to swallow a red-hot iron ball,
blazing like a crest of fire,
than that one who is immoral should eat.
Unrestrained in the alms of the land.
The Story of the Merchant’s Son Khemaka (Dhp 309). Four states a heedless man [falls into]: [the state of a dog, a jackal, a crow, and a pig].
(Dhp 86) A man who is negligent [falls into] four conditions.
One who consorts with another's wife incurs these:
the acquisition of demerit, lack of restful sleep,
thirdly, blame, and fourthly, hell.
The gain of demerit, a miserable rebirth,
and the fleeting pleasure of one who is afraid with one who is afraid;
and the king inflicts a heavy punishment.
Therefore, a person should not pursue another's wife.
(The Story of the Harsh-speaking Bhikkhu; Dhp 311, PTS [2nd ed.
Dhp 87) Just as kusa grass, when wrongly grasped, [cuts the hand].
He cuts his very own hand;
the ascetic life, when wrongly grasped,
drags one toward hell.
Whatever action is lax, whatever vow is defiled,
and whatever holy life is dubious—
That does not bear great fruit.
If one should do it, let one do it; let one exert oneself with firm resolve.
For one who is lax in their wandering life stirs up even more dust.
(Dhp 314, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 88)
It is better that a misdeed be left undone,
for a misdeed brings remorse later;
it is better that a good deed be done.
That which, having done, one does not regret.
(The Story of Many Bhikkhus, Dhp 315; PTS 2nd ed.
Dhp 88) Just as a frontier city [is fortified],...
Like a drop [of water] on the inner and outer [palm],
thus guard yourselves;
let not the opportune moment pass you by.
For those who have let the opportune moment pass grieve when they are cast into hell.
(The Story of the Nigaṇṭhas, Dhp 316; PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 88)
They feel shame for what is not shameful,
and feel no shame for what is shameful; through their adoption of wrong views, they are lost.
Beings go to an evil destination:
those who see danger where there is no danger, and those who see no danger where there is danger.
Through the adoption of wrong view, beings go to an evil destination.
The Story of the Disciple of a Heretic (Dhp 318, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 89)
Those who perceive the blameless as blameworthy,
and the blameworthy as blameless,
through their adherence to wrong view—
Beings go to a miserable destination if they perceive the blameworthy as blameworthy and the blameless as blameless.
(Dhp 319, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 89)
By undertaking right view, beings go to a good destination.

The Minor Collection:
The Way of the Dhamma, Chapter on the Elephant (Nāgavagga)
Like an elephant in battle [endures] an arrow shot from a bow, so am I. (Dhp 320)
I shall endure harsh words,
for the majority of people are ill-behaved; they lead the tamed one to the assembly.
The tamed man mounts the king;
the tamed is the best among humans—
he who endures abuse.
Better than mules, even thoroughbred Sindhu horses,
and great tusker elephants, are those who are well-tamed.
One who has tamed themselves is better than those.
[The Story of the Former Elephant Trainer and the Monk] (Dhp 323, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 90):
Indeed, not by these vehicles...
One may go to a region never before reached;
as one who is well-tamed goes by means of oneself, so does the tamed one go by means of the tamed.
The Story of the Worn-out Brahmin’s Son (Dhp 324, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 91):
Like the elephant named Dhanapāla, who is difficult to restrain when his temples are in rut;
Bound, the elephant does not eat his morsel;
he remembers the Nāga forest. (Pasenadi of Kosala)
When one is slothful and a great eater,
sleeping and tossing about in bed like a great boar fattened on fodder—
The dull-witted one enters the womb again and again.
This story of the novice Sānu (Dhp 326, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 91):
"In the past, this mind wandered on its wanderings..."
Moving according to its own will, wherever it desires, and as it pleases—
today I shall thoroughly restrain that [mind],
just as one who holds a goad restrains a rutting elephant.
Be devoted to heedfulness; guard your own minds well.
Lift yourselves out of the difficult pass, like an elephant stuck in the mud.
(Sambahulabhikkhu-vatthu, Dhp 328; PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 92)
If one should find a prudent companion,
a steadfast friend who lives virtuously and walks with one,
overcoming all dangers—
One should practice with a mind joyful and mindful.
But if one does not find a wise companion to walk with— one who is steadfast, lives virtuously, and is intelligent— [one should rather go alone].
Having abandoned his conquered kingdom like a king, one should wander alone like an elephant in the Matanga forest.
The life of solitude is better. (Dhp 330, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 92)
There is no companionship with fools;

For a person who wanders heedlessly,
craving grows like a creeping vine;
he drifts from one state of existence to another.
Like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest, this wretched craving, which clings in the world, is what one must endure. (Dhp 335, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 94)
His sorrows increase like grass after rain,
for he who endures this wretched existence.
Craving in the world is difficult to overcome;
from it sorrows fall away like drops of water from a lotus leaf.
I say this to you for your welfare,
all you who have gathered here:
dig up the root of craving.
As one seeking usira grass cuts down the bīraṇa;
may Māra not break you again and again, as he did the reed and the cane.
Just as a tree, though cut down, grows up once more if its root remains unharmed and firm;
Even so, as long as the underlying tendency to craving has not been uprooted,
this suffering arises again and again.
For one whose thirty-six streams [of craving]— (Dhp 339, PTS (2nd ed) Dhp 95)
Powerful and pleasing to the mind,
intentions based on lust carry one away into wrong view.
Everywhere streams flow; a creeper grows and stands there.
Having seen that creeper grown, [one should reflect: "I too am like this."
Cut off at the root with wisdom those streams and endearments,
those delights that arise for a person.
Those people who are attached to pleasure and seek after happiness surely go to birth and old age;
beings are led on by craving. (Dhp 342, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 96)
They wander about like a trapped hare;
bound by the fetters of attachment,
they encounter suffering again and again for a long time.
Led by craving, beings run about like a trapped hare;
therefore, one should dispel craving.
One who desires his own dispassion—
like the case of the wandering monk (Dhp 344, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 96)—
he who has escaped from the forest yet is intent upon the forest.
Freed from the forest, he runs back to the very forest;
behold this person here:
though released, he runs back to his bonds.
The wise do not call that a strong bond which is made of iron, wood, or rope; [but rather that which is made of desire].
The passion and infatuation for jeweled earrings, and the longing for children and wives—this, the wise say, is a firm bond. (Dhp 346, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 97)
Carrying away, loose, and difficult to release—
having cut even this asunder, they go forth as wanderers,
free from longing, having abandoned sensual pleasure.
Those who are stained by passion follow the stream like a spider following the web it has woven for itself.
Having cut even this as well, the wise go on, free from longing, having abandoned all suffering.
(The Story of Ugga Senāpati, Dhp 348; PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 98)
Relinquish what is before, relinquish what is behind,
and relinquish the middle; having reached the further shore of existence,
with a mind liberated in every respect—

Wealth destroys the fool.

Restraint in speech is good;

Restrained in hand, restrained in foot,

One who is contented—him they call a bhikkhu.

That bhikkhu who is restrained in speech...
Speaking with measured words and free from agitation,
he illuminates both the meaning and the Dhamma;

Delighting in the Dhamma, rejoicing in the Dhamma, reflecting upon the Dhamma;

One should not despise one's own gain,
nor should one live envying the gains of others;

He does not attain concentration.
Even if a bhikkhu has few gains, if he does not despise those gains; (Dhp 366, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 102)
The gods indeed praise that person who lives pure and is untiring.
*Pañcaggadāyakabrāhmaṇavatthu* (Dhp 367, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 102)
He for whom there is no sense of "mine" in name-and-form in every respect does not grieve over what is non-existent.
He indeed is called a "bhikkhu.

That bhikkhu who dwells in loving-kindness...
Having faith in the Buddha’s teaching,
one shall attain the state of peace,
the bliss that is the stilling of all conditioned formations.
Bail out this boat, O bhikkhu; once bailed out, it will go swiftly for you.
Cut off both lust and hatred.
Then you will attain Nibbāna.
Cut off five, abandon five, and cultivate five further states. (Dhp 370, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 103)
The bhikkhu who has transcended the five attachments is called "one who has crossed the flood.
Meditate, bhikkhu; do not be negligent. (Dhp 371, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 103)
Let not your mind delight in the strands of sensual pleasure;
let not the heedless man swallow a ball of iron while intoxicated,
crying out as he burns, "This is suffering!"
There is no meditation for one without wisdom, and there is no wisdom for one who does not meditate;
but in whom both meditation and wisdom exist,
[that person is truly wise].
He is indeed close to Nibbāna—when a bhikkhu of peaceful mind has entered an empty dwelling. (Dhp 373, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 104)
Supernatural joy arises for one who clearly sees the Dhamma rightly;
from whatever [aspect] one contemplates it, (Dhp 374, PTS (2nd ed. Dhp 104)
One who perceives the arising and passing away of the aggregates attains rapture and joy;
that is the deathless for those who understand it.
In this regard, this is the beginning for a wise bhikkhu here:
guarding the sense faculties and contentment.
And restraint according to the Pātimokkha;
associate with virtuous friends who are pure in livelihood and free from sloth.
One should be hospitable by nature and skilled in conduct;
thereafter, one should abound in gladness.
He will make an end of suffering.
The Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus (Dhp 377, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 105):
Like jasmine flowers...
He releases his softness;

Tranquil in body, tranquil in speech, and tranquil in mind,

The bhikkhu who has cast off worldly gain is called "one who is at peace.
The Story of the Elder Naṅgalakula (Dhp 379, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 105)
Exhort yourself by yourself, examine yourself by yourself;
thus guarded by yourself and possessed of mindfulness, you shall fare well.
You will dwell in happiness, O monk.
For oneself is indeed one's own protector; for who else could be the protector?
For oneself is one's own refuge;
therefore, one should restrain oneself,
as a merchant restrains a noble horse.
The story of the Elder Vakkali (Dhp 381, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 106):
A bhikkhu who abounds in joy, having faith in the Buddha’s teaching;
One shall attain the peaceful state, the bliss that is the subsiding of all conditioned formations.
The Story of the Novice Sumanas (Dhp 382, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 106)
Indeed, that young bhikkhu who applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching illuminates this world.
Like the moon released from clouds.

The Story of the Elder Sāriputta (Dhp 392, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 109):
From whom one may learn the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One;
One should honor him with reverence,
as a Brahmin honors the sacred fire-offering.
(The Story of the Brahmans with Matted Hair, Dhp 393)
One does not become a brahmin by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth;
he in whom there is truth and righteousness—
He is pure, and he is a brahmin.
The Story of the Deceitful Brahmin (Dhp 394, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 110):
"Of what use are matted locks to you, O dull-witted one?"
What use have you for a garment of antelope skin?
Your interior is dense with defilement,
yet you polish only the exterior.
A person who wears rag-robes, emaciated,
with veins showing all over the body;
One who meditates alone in the forest—
him I call a brahmin.
(Ekabrāhmaṇavatthu, Dhp 396)
And I do not call one a brahmin by birth,
born from a mother’s womb;
he is merely called "one who says 'bho'."
If one still possesses anything,
yet is without possessions and without grasping—
him I call a brahmin.
Having severed all fetters, he who indeed does not tremble—
One who has transcended attachment and is disjoined from it— him I call a brahmin.
(The Story of the Two Brahmins, Dhp 398)
Having cut through the thong, the strap,
the tether, and the traces along with the yoke-halter—
the Buddha who has removed the crossbar—
Him I call a brahmin.
The Story of Bhāradvāja the Abusive (Dhp 399, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 111):
Abuse, killing, and imprisonment—
He who, being free from hatred, practices endurance—
possessing the power of patience as his army—
it is him that I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Sāriputta (Dhp 400, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 111):
One who is free from anger, steadfast, virtuous, and free from pride;
One who is self-controlled and bears his final body—him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā (Dhp 401, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 112)
Like water on a lotus leaf,
like a mustard seed on the tip of an awl,
he who is not smeared by sensual pleasures—
Him I call a brahmin.
The Story of a Certain Brahmin (Dhp 402, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 112):
He who understands suffering...
Right here, having exhausted himself,
with the burden laid down and detached from bonds—
him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Bhikkhunī Khemā (Dhp 403, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 112):
To one of profound wisdom, possessed of intelligence, skilled in discerning the path and the non-path;
One who has attained the highest goal—him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Tissa of the Mountain Cave (Dhp 404, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 112)
Unassociated with householders and with both types of renunciants alike,
wandering without a home and possessing few desires—
Him I call a brahmin.
[The Case of a Certain Bhikkhu] (Dhp 405, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 113):
Having laid aside the rod toward all living beings,
Among those that move and those that are stationary,
he who neither kills nor causes to kill—
him I call a brahmin.
One who is unprovoked among those who provoke,
and who has attained peace among those who wield the rod of violence;
One who is without grasping amidst those who grasp—I call him a brahmin.
(The Story of the Elder Mahāpanthaka; Dhp 407, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 113)
For one from whom lust and hatred,
pride and hypocrisy have fallen away like mustard seeds from the point of an awl—
Him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Pilindavaccha (Dhp 408, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 113):
One who speaks without harshness and with clarity...
One should utter speech that is true;
one by whom no one is reviled—
him I call a brahmin.
Whatever exists here— whether long or short,
subtle or gross, beautiful or ugly—
In this world, he does not take what is not given;
him I call a brahmin.
(The Story of the Elder Sāriputta, Dhp 410)
He for whom no desires exist,
neither in this world nor in the world beyond— him,
free from longing and detached, [I call a brahmin].
Him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna (Dhp 411).
He for whom no attachments exist...
Having known this, free from doubt,
and having reached the state that plunges into the Deathless—
him I call a brahmin.
He who here has transcended both merit and evil, having passed beyond both attachments;
One who is sorrowless, stainless, and pure—
him I call a brahmin.
(The Story of the Elder Candābha, Dhp 413)
Like the moon, stainless and pure,
serene and undisturbed,
with delight and becoming utterly exhausted.
Him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Sīvali (Dhp 414, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 115):
He who [crosses] this mire, this difficult path...
He has transcended the delusion of saṃsāra;
having crossed over and reached the further shore, he is a meditator,
unshaken and free from doubt.
One who has attained Nibbāna without clinging—him I call a brahmin.
(The Story of the Elder Sundarasamudda; Dhp 415, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 115)
The one who, having abandoned sensual desires,
wanders forth as a homeless renunciant—
him whose existence in sense-desire has been utterly exhausted.
Him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Jaṭila (Dhp 416, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 116):
He who, having abandoned craving here in this world...
One who wanders homeless as a wanderer,
with craving and becoming utterly exhausted—
that person I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Jotika:
He who, having abandoned craving,
goes forth as a homeless wanderer;
One whose craving and becoming are completely destroyed—him I call a brahmin.
(The Story of the Elder Naṭaputtaka) (Dhp 417, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 116)
Having abandoned human bondage,
he has transcended divine bondage;
he is dissociated from all bonds.
Him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Naṭaputtaka (Dhp 418, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 116):
Having abandoned both delight and aversion, [him I call a brahmin].
Who has become cooled and is free from acquisitions;
the hero who overcomes the entire world—
him I call a brahmin.
The story of the Elder Vaṅgīsa (Dhp 419, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 117):
He who fully understands the passing away and the rebirth of beings;
One who is unattached, well-gone, and awakened—him I call a brahmin.
Whose destination they do not know... (Dhp 420, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 117)
Gods, gandhabbas, and humans—
him who has destroyed the taints, the arahant,
him I call a brahmin.
The Story of the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā (Dhp 421, PTS [2nd ed. Dhp 117):
He for whom there is nothing whatsoever in the past, in the future, and in the present;
One who possesses nothing and takes nothing—that person I call a brahmin.
(The Story of the Elder Aṅgulimāla; Dhp 422, PTS 2nd ed. Dhp 117)
To the bull-like, preeminent hero,
the great seer who has conquered,
the unshakable, the washed-cleansed Buddha—
Him I call a brahmin.
(The Devahita Brahmin Story, Dhp 423; PTS 2nd ed., Dhp 117) He who knows his former abodes...
He sees both heaven and the states of woe;
moreover, having reached the destruction of birth,
the sage is perfected in direct knowledge.
One who has brought all undertakings to their conclusion—him I call a brahmin.
